A single stellar spectrum has measurements at thousands of wavelength bins, and a galaxy image has tens of thousands of pixels. Even a simple stellar catalog can list dozens of elemental abundances. Yet we often suspect that only a few physical parameters determine these measurements. We want to find a few combinations of the measurements that explain most of the variation in the data.

Stellar spectra with thousands of wavelength points are mainly determined by the effective temperature, the surface gravity and the metallicity. Galaxy morphologies look complex but often come from a few formation and evolution processes. The chemical compositions of stars in a cluster, measured in many elements, usually come from a few nucleosynthesis processes.

Principal component analysis (PCA) is our first unsupervised method, because it uses no target variable. It finds a lower-dimensional representation of high-dimensional data that keeps as much information as possible. It uses the covariance matrix of Chapter 3 and linear algebra to find the directions of maximum variation.

Suppose that a few underlying factors determine the data. Then most of the variation should lie along a few directions in the data space. PCA finds these directions, which are the principal components, so we can describe each object with far fewer numbers.

Reducing the dimension, also called dimensionality reduction, helps with three problems of astronomical data. First, data with more than two or three dimensions are hard to visualize, so we can inspect them only in projection. Second, the computing cost grows quickly with the number of dimensions. Third, inference becomes harder in many dimensions, because the available data become sparse compared with the volume of the space. This is the curse of dimensionality. For example, 100 objects fill the 10 bins of one feature, but 10 features with 10 bins each make \(10^{10}\) bins and most stay empty.

In this chapter we derive PCA as a constrained optimization problem (Sections 10.2 and 10.3). We show that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by their eigenvalues. The singular value decomposition (SVD) of Section 10.8 makes the computation efficient when there are fewer objects than features.

10.1 PCA Fundamentals

Consider a data set of \(N\) astronomical objects with \(D\) measurements each. The data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) has one object per row and one feature per column. For stellar spectroscopy, \(N\) is the number of observed stars and \(D\) is the number of wavelength bins. For galaxy photometry, the features can be magnitudes in different bands.

Not all directions in this \(D\)-dimensional feature space are equally informative. Along some directions the objects differ by large amounts, and these directions separate one object from another. Along other directions the data vary little. These directions can hold measurement noise, redundant information or properties that do not distinguish between objects.

Two Perspectives on Dimensionality Reduction

PCA can be described in two ways that give the same solution. The first looks for the directions in the high-dimensional space along which the data vary the most, and projects the data onto them. Directions of larger variance carry more information about the structure of the data. Here we use information in the loose sense of variance, the spread of the data along a direction. In stellar spectra, directions of maximum variance can match physical differences in temperature, metallicity or surface gravity. In galaxy photometry they can follow differences in mass, star formation rate or morphology.

The second way looks for a lower-dimensional representation of the data. We map the lower-dimensional representation of each object back to the original space, and the result is its reconstruction. The average squared distance between the data points and their reconstructions should be as small as possible. This view preserves the overall structure of the data cloud. Because the two ways agree, PCA finds the lower-dimensional representation that keeps the most information among linear projections to a given number of dimensions.

Notation and Centering

We begin with the notation and one simplifying assumption. The observations are the vectors \(\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N \in \mathbb{R}^D\), and \(\mathbf{x}_i^T\) is the \(i\)-th row of \(\mathbf{X}\). We write \(\mathbf{x}\) for one object drawn from the data set, for example one star.

To simplify the derivation, we assume that the data are centered, so that their average is zero \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{0}. \]Here \(\mathbb{E}\) denotes the average over the data set. Astronomical data rarely have a clear zero point, so we subtract the sample mean \(\overline{\mathbf{x}}\) of the original observations from each observation \[ \mathbf{x}_i' = \mathbf{x}_i - \overline{\mathbf{x}}. \]

We took the same step in Chapter 6, where it removed the intercept. From now on, \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and \(\mathbf{X}\) hold the centered data, and \(\overline{\mathbf{x}}\) stays the mean of the original observations. Centered values are deviations from the mean, so we can read the variance directly as a measure of information.

Vector Projections and Basis Decomposition

PCA rests on vector projection. Projecting a vector \(\mathbf{x}\) onto a unit vector \(\mathbf{b}\) in \(D\) dimensions gives \[ \widehat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b})\mathbf{b}. \]

The scalar \(\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}\) measures how far \(\mathbf{x}\) extends along \(\mathbf{b}\), and multiplying it by \(\mathbf{b}\) gives a vector along \(\mathbf{b}\) of that length. In Figure 10.1 the bracket along the line has length \(\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}\). The dashed segment from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{b}\), so \(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\) is the point on the line closest to \(\mathbf{x}\). The distance \(\|\mathbf{x}-\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\|\) is the reconstruction error of this projection. This closest-point property matters for PCA, because we seek basis vectors that minimize the sum of squared reconstruction errors across the data points.

This concept extends to multiple dimensions through basis decomposition. With a complete set of orthonormal basis vectors \(\{\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_D\}\), which are mutually perpendicular unit vectors, we can write any vector \(\mathbf{x}\) as \[ \mathbf{x} = \sum_{m=1}^D (\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{b}_m)\mathbf{b}_m. \]This representation uses \(D\) coefficients, one for the projection onto each basis vector. In PCA we look for a basis in which most of the variance of the data lies along the first few basis vectors.

In matrix form, let \(\mathbf{B}_M\) hold the first \(M\) basis vectors as columns \[ \mathbf{B}_M = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{b}_M \end{bmatrix}, \] and let \(\mathbf{B}_R\) hold the remaining basis vectors \[ \mathbf{B}_R = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}_{M+1} & \mathbf{b}_{M+2} & \cdots & \mathbf{b}_D \end{bmatrix}. \]

The projection coefficients form the vectors \[ \mathbf{z}_M = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_1 \\ \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_M \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{z}_R = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_{M+1} \\ \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_{M+2} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_D \end{bmatrix}. \]

We treat \(\mathbf{x}\) as a random vector, so the coefficients \(\mathbf{z}_M\) and \(\mathbf{z}_R\) are random vectors too. The coefficient \(z_j = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_j\) is the coordinate of \(\mathbf{x}\) along \(\mathbf{b}_j\). The data are centered, so the coefficients have zero expectation \[ \mathbb{E}[z_j] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{b}_j] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}]^T \mathbf{b}_j = \mathbf{0}^T \mathbf{b}_j = 0. \]The variance of a coefficient is therefore its mean square value, \(\mathbb{E}[z_j^2]\), which measures the spread of the data along \(\mathbf{b}_j\).

With this notation the complete decomposition is \[ \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{B}_M\mathbf{z}_M + \mathbf{B}_R\mathbf{z}_R. \]

PCA keeps only the first term, which gives the lower-dimensional approximation \[ \widehat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{B}_M\mathbf{z}_M. \]

The difference between the data and the approximation is the reconstruction error \[ \mathbf{x} - \widehat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{B}_R\mathbf{z}_R. \]Figure 10.2 shows an example with \(D = 3\) and \(M = 2\). The data in panel (a) lie around a two-dimensional plane in three-dimensional space. The dashed segments are the reconstruction errors. PCA finds the lower-dimensional plane that best preserves the information in the data.

Equivalence of the Two Perspectives

The equivalence follows from the total variance of the centered data \[ \text{Total Variance} = \mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{x}\|^2] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x}]. \]

In the orthonormal basis \(\{\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_D\}\) we have \(\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 = \sum_{m=1}^D z_m^2\), so the total variance becomes \[ \text{Total Variance} = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{m=1}^D z_m^2\right] = \sum_{m=1}^M \mathbb{E}[z_m^2] + \sum_{j=M+1}^D \mathbb{E}[z_j^2]. \]The first term is the variance carried by the first \(M\) basis vectors. The second term is the expected squared reconstruction error. The total variance does not depend on the basis, so the two terms add up to a fixed total. The \(M\) orthonormal directions that carry the most variance therefore leave the smallest reconstruction error.

10.2 PCA as an Optimization Problem

We now write this goal as an optimization problem. We need basis vectors \(\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_M\) that carry the maximum variance and stay orthonormal. We start with the first principal component, the direction that holds the most variance. Once we solve this case, we can extend the approach to the later components.

Consider the projection of the data onto a vector \(\mathbf{b}_1\). For a data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) the projection coefficient is \(z_{1i} = \mathbf{x}_i^T\mathbf{b}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{x}_i\). We want the direction \(\mathbf{b}_1\) that maximizes the variance of these coefficients \[ \text{Var}[z_1] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N z_{1i}^2. \]

For centered data the covariance matrix of Chapter 3 reduces to the second moment \[ \mathbf{S} = \text{Cov}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^T] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^T = \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}. \]We write \(\mathbf{S}\) instead of the \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) of Chapter 3, because \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) later holds the singular values.

To connect this variance to the covariance matrix, we use the formula for the covariance of a linear transformation (Chapter 3). If \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) for a random vector \(\mathbf{x}\) and a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), then \[ \text{Cov}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{A} \cdot \text{Cov}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{A}^T. \]Here \(z_1 = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{x}\) is such a transformation with \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{b}_1^T\). The variable \(z_1\) is a scalar, so its variance is \[ \text{Var}[z_1] = \mathbf{b}_1^T \cdot \text{Cov}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{b}_1 = \mathbf{b}_1^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{b}_1. \]This expression connects the variance of the projected data to \(\mathbf{S}\). Finding the direction of maximum variance reduces to finding the vector \(\mathbf{b}_1\) that maximizes the quadratic form \(\mathbf{b}_1^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{b}_1\).

The Need for Constraints

Without a constraint the problem is ill-defined. Multiplying any vector \(\mathbf{b}_1\) by a constant \(c > 1\) gives the variance \[ \text{Var}[z_1'] = (c\mathbf{b}_1)^T \mathbf{S} (c\mathbf{b}_1) = c^2 \mathbf{b}_1^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{b}_1 = c^2 \text{Var}[z_1]. \]The variance grows without limit as the length of \(\mathbf{b}_1\) grows, while the direction stays the same. Only the direction matters for the axis of maximum variance, so we constrain the length.

We require \(\mathbf{b}_1\) to be a unit vector \[ \|\mathbf{b}_1\|^2 = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 = 1. \]With unit length, the variance depends only on the direction of \(\mathbf{b}_1\). The optimization problem becomes \[ \max_{\mathbf{b}_1} \mathbf{b}_1^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{b}_1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 = 1. \]Finding the first principal component is a constrained optimization problem. Such problems appear in physics, engineering and economics and are typically solved with the method of Lagrange multipliers.

10.3 Lagrange Multipliers

The method of Lagrange multipliers finds candidates for the extrema of a function under constraints.

Without constraints we find extrema where the gradient vanishes, \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = 0\), because the function stops changing in all directions. Here \(\mathbf{x}\) is the vector of all variables of \(f\), and it is not the data vector of the previous sections. The function \(f\) returns one number. We did this for maximum likelihood estimation in earlier chapters.

With a constraint we may use only points that satisfy \(g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\). A constraint \(h(\mathbf{x}) = c\) has this form with \(g(\mathbf{x}) = h(\mathbf{x}) - c\). Inequality constraints also exist, but PCA does not need them. The point where \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = 0\) may lie off the set \(g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\), so we need a new condition.

The constraint \(g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\) defines a constraint surface, and we must stay on it. For PCA the constraint is \(g(\mathbf{b}_1) = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 - 1 = 0\), which restricts the search to unit vectors. This constraint surface is the unit sphere, and it removes one degree of freedom.

Geometric Intuition

We find the new condition geometrically. Consider a function \(f(x,y)\) of two variables, whose maximum or minimum we want under the constraint \(g(x,y) = 0\). We can picture \(f\) as a surface with hills and valleys above the \((x,y)\) plane and the constraint as a path in that plane.

The path is one-dimensional, because \(g(x,y) = 0\) removes one degree of freedom from the plane. For example, \(g(x,y) = x + y - 1 = 0\) is a straight line. We look for the point on the path where \(f\) reaches its extremum.

The gradient \(\nabla f\) points in the direction of steepest ascent of \(f\). If \(\nabla f\) had a component along the path, we could stay on the constraint and increase \(f\) by moving one way along the path. Moving the other way would decrease \(f\). At a constrained extremum no such moves exist, so \(\nabla f\) is perpendicular to the path.

But what direction is perpendicular to the constraint path? The function \(g\) is constant, equal to zero, along the path, so a small step along the path leaves \(g\) unchanged to first order. Such a step is perpendicular to \(\nabla g\), the direction of steepest ascent of \(g\). So \(\nabla g\) is perpendicular to the path. Figure 10.3 shows this for \(g(x,y) = x + y - 1\), where the arrows of \(\nabla g\) cross the contours at right angles.

At a constrained extremum, both gradients are perpendicular to the path. The path has one dimension fewer than the space, so the vectors perpendicular to it lie along one line. The two gradients are therefore parallel \[ \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \lambda \nabla g(\mathbf{x}), \] where \(\lambda\) is the Lagrange multiplier, the scalar that relates them. This parallel condition is the core of the method.

Figure 10.4 shows both gradients for \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) and the line \(g(x,y) = x + y - 1 = 0\). The figure also marks the unconstrained minimum at the origin, which the line does not contain.

The Lagrangian Formulation

We turn the constrained problem into a search for critical points of a function with one extra variable, the multiplier \(\lambda\). This function is the Lagrangian \[ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda g(\mathbf{x}). \]Its critical points, where all partial derivatives vanish, are the candidate solutions of the constrained problem. We therefore solve an unconstrained problem in a slightly larger space.

The gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{x}\) gives \[ \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L} = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda \nabla g(\mathbf{x}) = 0. \] Rearranging gives \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \lambda \nabla g(\mathbf{x})\) again, which agrees with the geometric argument.

The derivative with respect to \(\lambda\) gives \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = -g(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \Rightarrow g(\mathbf{x}) = 0. \] This is the constraint itself, so the critical points lie on the constraint surface. Solving the two conditions together gives all candidates for constrained extrema.

A Simple Example

We now solve the example of Figure 10.4. We want the minimum of \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) under the constraint \(g(x,y) = x + y - 1 = 0\). The Lagrangian is \[ \mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda) = x^2 + y^2 - \lambda(x + y - 1). \]

Setting the partial derivatives to zero gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} &= 2x - \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow x = \frac{\lambda}{2}, \\ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y} &= 2y - \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow y = \frac{\lambda}{2}, \\ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} &= -(x + y - 1) = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 1. \end{aligned}\]The first two equations give \(x = y\). The constraint then gives \[ x + x = 1 \Rightarrow x = y = \frac{1}{2}. \]

The value at this point is \(f(1/2, 1/2) = (1/2)^2 + (1/2)^2 = 1/2\). The Lagrange equations are necessary conditions. All constrained extrema satisfy them, but a point that satisfies them need not be an extremum. Here only one point satisfies them, namely \((1/2, 1/2)\). A minimum exists on the line, because \(f\) grows without bound along it in both directions, so this point is the minimum. With several critical points we would need further analysis to find the extremum.

Multiple Constraints

Lagrange multipliers extend to several constraints \(g_1(\mathbf{x}) = 0\), \(g_2(\mathbf{x}) = 0\), …, \(g_K(\mathbf{x}) = 0\). The condition becomes \[ \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \lambda_1 \nabla g_1(\mathbf{x}) + \lambda_2 \nabla g_2(\mathbf{x}) + \ldots + \lambda_K \nabla g_K(\mathbf{x}). \]

With several constraints we are restricted to the intersection of all constraint surfaces, a surface of lower dimension called a manifold. At a constrained extremum, \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\) must be perpendicular to this manifold. Otherwise we could move along the manifold, satisfy all constraints and change \(f\).

A direction tangent to the manifold is tangent to all constraint surfaces, so it is perpendicular to all constraint gradients \(\nabla g_k(\mathbf{x})\). The vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\) must therefore lie in the span of these gradients. It is a linear combination of them, with the multipliers \(\lambda_k\) as coefficients.

The Lagrangian for this case is \[ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_K) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda_1 g_1(\mathbf{x}) - \ldots - \lambda_K g_K(\mathbf{x}). \] Setting its partial derivatives to zero gives the constraint equations and the gradient condition above.

10.4 Solving PCA with Lagrange Multipliers

We now apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to the first principal component. Recall that our objective is to maximize the variance of the projected data. In symbols, we maximize \(f(\mathbf{b}_1) = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1\) under the constraint \(g(\mathbf{b}_1) = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 - 1 = 0\).

The Lagrangian of the problem is \[ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{b}_1, \lambda_1) = \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1 - \lambda_1(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 - 1). \]Setting the derivative with respect to \(\lambda_1\) to zero gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\lambda_1} = -(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 - 1) = 0. \end{aligned}\] This is the constraint \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 = 1\), so \(\mathbf{b}_1\) is a unit vector.

For the derivative with respect to \(\mathbf{b}_1\) we need two results of matrix calculus. For a symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{S}\), the gradient of \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1\) is \(2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1\). The gradient of \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1\) is \(2\mathbf{b}_1\). To see the first result, write the quadratic form as \(\sum_{j,l} S_{jl} b_{1j} b_{1l}\). Its derivative with respect to \(b_{1k}\) is \(2\sum_j S_{kj} b_{1j}\), because \(S_{jl} = S_{lj}\), and this is the \(k\)-th component of \(2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1\). Therefore \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}_1} = 2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1 - 2\lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1 = 0. \end{aligned}\] Dividing by 2 and rearranging gives \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1. \end{aligned}\]

The Eigenvalue Equation

When \(\mathbf{S}\) acts on \(\mathbf{b}_1\), the result is \(\mathbf{b}_1\) again, multiplied by \(\lambda_1\). A vector with this property is called an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\), and the multiplier \(\lambda_1\) is its eigenvalue. Any solution \(\mathbf{b}_1\) of these equations is therefore an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\). A search over all unit vectors becomes a search among the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\), which we can compute with standard linear algebra.

Eigenvectors of a covariance matrix have a geometric meaning. When we apply the matrix to the vectors of a unit circle, most vectors change both direction and length. An eigenvector keeps its direction, and the matrix only scales it by the eigenvalue. In Figure 10.5 the eigenvectors \(\mathbf{b}_1\) and \(\mathbf{b}_2\) of a two-dimensional covariance matrix keep their direction. The vector \(\mathbf{u}\) is not an eigenvector, and it turns.

This is what the equation \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1\) says. This property makes eigenvectors good candidates for our principal components.

A covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is real and symmetric, so its eigenvalues are real and eigenvectors of different eigenvalues are orthogonal. We can also choose \(D\) orthonormal eigenvectors that span the \(D\)-dimensional space. Collecting them as the columns of \(\mathbf{B}\) gives the spectral decomposition \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{B}^T\). Here \(\mathbf{B}\) is the \(D \times D\) orthogonal matrix and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is the diagonal matrix of the eigenvalues. The principal components will come from these eigenvectors, so they form an orthonormal basis.

Connecting Eigenvalues to Variance

Which of the \(D\) orthonormal eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\) maximizes the variance?

To decide, we substitute an eigenvector \(\mathbf{b}_1\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) into the variance of the projected data \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}[z_1] &= \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1 \\ &= \mathbf{b}_1^T(\lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1) \\ &= \lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 \\ &= \lambda_1. \end{aligned}\] In the last step we used \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 = 1\), because \(\mathbf{b}_1\) is a unit vector.

The same steps apply to any unit eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\), so the variance along an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue. This connection between statistical variance and algebraic eigenvalues justifies our approach to PCA.

A maximizer of the variance is an eigenvector, and its variance equals its eigenvalue. The first principal component is therefore an eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, and the data vary most along it. Figure 10.6 shows the data and the covariance ellipse, which extends two standard deviations along each eigenvector, for a two-dimensional example. The eigenvector \(\mathbf{b}_1\) lies along the long axis of the ellipse, where the data spread most. The second principal component is orthogonal to the first.

10.5 Higher-Order Principal Components

The first component rarely represents high-dimensional data well. We therefore look for further components that carry the remaining variance. The second principal component is a direction \(\mathbf{b}_2\) with two properties. It carries the maximum variance that the first component has not explained. It is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{b}_1\), so that \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_2 = 0\).

Orthogonality is an assumption of PCA. With only the unit length constraint, the direction of maximum variance is \(\mathbf{b}_1\) again, so the second direction needs another condition. Orthogonality keeps the calculation tractable and makes each principal component carry a unique aspect of the variation in the data.

Solving for the Second Component

The second component solves another constrained optimization problem \[ \max_{\mathbf{b}_2} \mathbf{b}_2^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{b}_2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{b}_2^T\mathbf{b}_2 = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_2 = 0. \]

We use Lagrange multipliers again, now with two constraints. The multiplier \(\lambda_2\) belongs to the unit length constraint and \(\mu\) to the orthogonality constraint \[ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{b}_2, \lambda_2, \mu) = \mathbf{b}_2^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_2 - \lambda_2(\mathbf{b}_2^T\mathbf{b}_2 - 1) - \mu(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_2). \]Setting the derivative with respect to \(\mathbf{b}_2\) to zero gives \[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}_2} = 2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_2 - 2\lambda_2\mathbf{b}_2 - \mu\mathbf{b}_1 = 0. \]

To solve this equation, we multiply from the left by \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\) \[ \mathbf{b}_1^T(2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_2 - 2\lambda_2\mathbf{b}_2 - \mu\mathbf{b}_1) = 0. \] Here \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_2 = 0\) by the orthogonality constraint, and \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_1 = 1\) because \(\mathbf{b}_1\) is a unit vector. The equation becomes \[ 2\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_2 - \mu = 0. \]

Since \(\mathbf{b}_1\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\), we have \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1\). The matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is symmetric, so the transpose gives \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{S} = \lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1^T\). Substituting this gives \[ 2\lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_2 - \mu = 0. \] Here \(\mathbf{b}_1^T\mathbf{b}_2 = 0\), so \(\mu = 0\). The derivative equation then reduces to \(2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_2 - 2\lambda_2\mathbf{b}_2 = 0\), which gives \[ \mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{b}_2. \]

So \(\mathbf{b}_2\) is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\), and the orthogonality constraint makes it differ from \(\mathbf{b}_1\). As before, the variance along \(\mathbf{b}_2\) is the eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\). To maximize it, we choose \(\mathbf{b}_2\) as an eigenvector with the second largest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{S}\).

The pattern we observed extends to the later principal components. For the \(m\)-th component we would need to solve \[ \max_{\mathbf{b}_m} \mathbf{b}_m^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{b}_m \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{b}_m^T\mathbf{b}_m = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{b}_k^T\mathbf{b}_m = 0 \quad \text{for all } k < m. \]

We expect that the \(m\)-th principal component is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with the \(m\)-th largest eigenvalue. Checking this for each \(m\) is long, so in the next section we prove it for all \(m\) at once by induction.

10.6 A Proof by Induction

Mathematical induction proves a statement for all components \(1, \ldots, D\) in one argument.

Induction has three steps.

  1. The base case proves the statement for the first value, usually \(m=1\).

  2. The inductive hypothesis assumes the statement for all values below a value \(M\).

  3. The inductive step proves that the statement then holds for \(M\).

If we complete all three steps, the statement holds for all values. Think of a row of dominoes. The first falls (base case), and each falls when the ones before it have fallen (inductive step), so all fall.

The \(m\)-th principal component is a unit vector that maximizes \(\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}\) among the vectors orthogonal to the first \(m-1\) components. The statement to prove for all \(m\) is that this vector is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with the \(m\)-th largest eigenvalue. We list the eigenvalues in descending order, \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_D\).

Base Case

We showed above that the first principal component \(\mathbf{b}_1\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\).

Inductive Hypothesis

Assume that for all \(m < M\) the \(m\)-th principal component \(\mathbf{b}_m\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with the \(m\)-th largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_m\).

Inductive Step

We must show that the \(M\)-th principal component \(\mathbf{b}_M\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with the \(M\)-th largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_M\).

Finding the \(M\)-th principal component is equivalent to finding the direction of maximum variance in the residual data. The residual data remain after we remove the projections onto the first \(M-1\) components.

To find the projection of the data onto the first \(M-1\) components, we recall that \(\mathbf{x}\) projects onto a unit vector \(\mathbf{b}_m\) as \((\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{b}_m)\mathbf{b}_m\). Applying it to each row of \(\mathbf{X}\) gives \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T\), the projection of all data points onto the \(m\)-th principal component.

The projection onto the subspace spanned by the first \(M-1\) principal components is the sum \[ \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T. \]Subtracting this projection from \(\mathbf{X}\) leaves the residual data, the part not explained by these components \[ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{X} - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T. \]

Let \(\mathbf{B}_{M-1} = [\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_{M-1}]\) be the matrix whose columns are the first \(M-1\) principal components. In matrix form the residual is \[ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T. \]The matrix \(\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\) projects onto the subspace spanned by the first \(M-1\) components. Subtracting this projection leaves the part of each data point that is orthogonal to the subspace. The residual \(\mathbf{r}_i\) of the data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is the \(i\)-th row of \(\mathbf{R}\), written as a column vector. Figure 10.7 shows a three-dimensional example with \(M = 2\), where the first \(M-1 = 1\) component is removed.

To find the direction of maximum variance in the residual data, we need to compute its covariance matrix \[ \mathbf{S}_R = \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}. \]Substituting \(\mathbf{R}\) and expanding gives \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_R &= \frac{1}{N}(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T)^T(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T) \\ &= \frac{1}{N}(\mathbf{X}^T - \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\mathbf{X}^T)(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T) \\ &= \frac{1}{N}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T - \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} \nonumber \\ &\quad + \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T). \end{aligned}\]Since \((1/N)\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{S}\), the original covariance matrix, this becomes \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_R &= \mathbf{S} - \mathbf{S}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T - \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T \mathbf{S} \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T. \end{aligned}\]

By the inductive hypothesis, \(\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\) holds the first \(M-1\) eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\), so \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{B}_{M-1} = \mathbf{B}_{M-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{M-1}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{M-1}\) is the diagonal matrix of the first \(M-1\) eigenvalues. Using this relation, the symmetry of \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\mathbf{B}_{M-1} = \mathrm{Id}\), the identity matrix, we find that each of the last three terms equals \(\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\). Their signs are minus, minus and plus, so they sum to \(-\mathbf{B}_{M-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{M-1}\mathbf{B}_{M-1}^T\), which is \(-\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}\lambda_m\mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T\). Therefore \[ \mathbf{S}_R = \mathbf{S} - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \lambda_m \mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T. \]The residual covariance matrix is the original matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) with the variance explained by the first \(M-1\) components subtracted.

To understand this relation, we examine how \(\mathbf{S}_R\) acts on the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\). The first \(M-1\) eigenvectors are \(\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_{M-1}\), and the others are \(\mathbf{b}_M, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_D\) with the eigenvalues \(\lambda_M \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_D\). For one of the first \(M-1\) eigenvectors, \(\mathbf{b}_k\) with \(k < M\), we find \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_R\mathbf{b}_k &= \mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_k - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \lambda_m \mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T\mathbf{b}_k \\ &= \lambda_k\mathbf{b}_k - \lambda_k \mathbf{b}_k = 0, \end{aligned}\] where we used the orthonormality of the eigenvectors.

For any other eigenvector, \(\mathbf{b}_j\) with \(j \geq M\), we find \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_R\mathbf{b}_j &= \mathbf{S}\mathbf{b}_j - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \lambda_m \mathbf{b}_m\mathbf{b}_m^T\mathbf{b}_j \\ &= \lambda_j\mathbf{b}_j - 0 = \lambda_j\mathbf{b}_j. \end{aligned}\]Therefore \(\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_{M-1}\) have eigenvalue 0 in \(\mathbf{S}_R\), and \(\mathbf{b}_M, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_D\) have the same eigenvalues in \(\mathbf{S}_R\) as in \(\mathbf{S}\). In Figure 10.7 the residuals have no extent along \(\mathbf{b}_1\), which matches the eigenvalue 0. In this figure, the largest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{S}_R\) is therefore the second largest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{S}\).

The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{S}_R\) are \[ \{0, 0, \ldots, 0, \lambda_M, \lambda_{M+1}, \ldots, \lambda_D\}, \] where the first \(M-1\) eigenvalues are zero and the others keep their values from \(\mathbf{S}\). The \(M\)-th principal component is the direction of maximum variance of the residual data. By the result for the first component, it is therefore the eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}_R\) with the largest eigenvalue, which is \(\lambda_M\). This eigenvector is \(\mathbf{b}_M\), the eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with the \(M\)-th largest eigenvalue.

This completes the induction. The principal components are the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\) in the order of their eigenvalues, from the largest to the smallest.

10.7 Implementing PCA

The derivation of PCA is long, but the algorithm is short. PCA takes six steps, and a single computation of the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\) gives all principal components at once.

  1. Center the data matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) of size \(N \times D\).

  2. Compute the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S} = (1/N)\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\).

  3. Compute the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{S}\).

  4. Sort the eigenvectors by decreasing eigenvalue.

  5. Take the first \(M\) eigenvectors as the columns of \(\mathbf{B}_M = [\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_M]\).

  6. Project the data onto this basis with \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_M\).

The matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\) has size \(N \times M\), and each row holds the coefficients of one data point in the principal component coordinates. These coefficients form the reduced representation. We can reconstruct approximations of the centered data with \(\widehat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{B}_M^T = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}_M\mathbf{B}_M^T\), the projection of \(\mathbf{X}\) onto the \(M\)-dimensional subspace of the principal components. The difference between \(\widehat{\mathbf{X}}\) and \(\mathbf{X}\) shows how much information the reduction loses.

Selecting the Number of Components

We must decide how many principal components to keep. For \(M = D\) the dimension does not decrease, and for a small \(M\) we lose information about the data. Our theory gives a criterion for selecting \(M\). By the induction proof, the principal components are eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\), and the variance along a component equals its eigenvalue (Section 10.4). The eigenvalues therefore rank the components by the variance they carry.

The total variance is the sum of the eigenvalues \[ \text{Total Variance} = \sum_{m=1}^D \lambda_m. \] The variance carried by the first \(M\) components is \[ \text{Captured Variance} = \sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m. \] The explained variance ratio of the first \(M\) components is the fraction of the total variance that they carry \[ \text{Explained Variance Ratio} = \frac{\sum_{m=1}^M \lambda_m}{\sum_{m=1}^D \lambda_m}. \]This ratio is a quantitative measure of how much information we retain after the dimension reduction. We can keep the smallest \(M\) for which this ratio reaches a threshold, typically 0.90, 0.95 or 0.99. The threshold depends on the requirements of the application.

A scree plot shows the eigenvalues, or their ratios to the total variance, against their index. The curve usually falls steeply at first and then flattens. The elbow, where the slope changes, can suggest a cutoff for \(M\).

Figure 10.8 shows a scree plot in panel (a) and the explained variance ratio of the first \(M\) components in panel (b). In panel (a) the ratios fall steeply up to the third component and are nearly flat after it. In panel (b) the thresholds 0.90, 0.95 and 0.99 need 3, 5 and 9 components.

Physical Interpretation of Components

The output of PCA gives information beyond dimension reduction. The eigenvalues show how much variance a component carries and how important a direction of variation is. The eigenvectors can often be interpreted in terms of the original features, since they show which combinations of measurements contribute most to the variation.

A spectrum has one entry per wavelength bin, so an eigenvector can be plotted like a spectrum. For stellar spectra, the first component might follow the overall flux level or the temperature. Later components might follow the metallicity or particular absorption lines. This ability to interpret components makes PCA useful for exploratory data analysis in astronomy.

PCA can help to identify the physical processes behind astronomical data. If a few components explain most of the variance, as in Figure 10.8, a few underlying parameters may determine the variation.

10.8 SVD for Efficient PCA

The algorithm above needs the \(D \times D\) covariance matrix and its eigenvectors. For high-dimensional data the cost of this step is large. A spectrum can have 10,000 wavelength bins, and an image can have tens of thousands of pixels. A time series can have thousands of time points. Diagonalizing a \(D \times D\) matrix needs of the order of \(D^3\) operations, written \(\mathcal{O}(D^3)\), so the cost grows quickly with \(D\). For \(D = 10^4\) the covariance matrix has \(10^8\) entries, which need about 800 megabytes of memory in double precision, where each number takes 8 bytes.

The SVD gives the same principal components at a lower cost when there are fewer objects than features. Many astronomical data sets have fewer objects than features.

The SVD Decomposition

The SVD theorem states that any matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) is the product of three matrices \[ \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T. \]The three matrices have these properties.

  • \(\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) has orthonormal columns, the left singular vectors.

  • \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) is a rectangular matrix whose entries are zero except on the main diagonal. The diagonal entries \(\Sigma_{mm} = \sigma_m\) are the singular values \(\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \ldots \geq \sigma_{\min(N,D)} \geq 0\), and we set \(\sigma_m = 0\) for \(m > \min(N,D)\).

  • \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) has orthonormal columns, the right singular vectors.

Each column of \(\mathbf{V}\) is a pattern of weights on the features. The matching column of \(\mathbf{U}\) gives the relative strength of that pattern in each object, and \(\sigma_m\) gives its overall strength.

Geometrically, the SVD splits any linear transformation into three simpler steps. The first is a rotation or reflection in the input space (\(\mathbf{V}^T\)). The second is a scaling along the coordinate axes (\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)). The third is a rotation or reflection in the output space (\(\mathbf{U}\)).

Cost of the SVD

The SVD of an \(N \times D\) matrix takes about \(\mathcal{O}(\min(ND^2, N^2D))\) operations when we compute only the first \(\min(N,D)\) columns of \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\), which PCA needs. This reduced form is called the economy-size SVD, and software routines provide it as an option. For a tall matrix with \(N > D\) the cost is \(\mathcal{O}(ND^2)\), and for a wide matrix with \(N < D\) it is \(\mathcal{O}(N^2D)\). In both cases we square the smaller dimension and multiply by the larger one. In this form, modern SVD routines adapt to the shape of the matrix automatically.

Take a spectroscopic survey with \(N = 1{,}000\) spectra and \(D = 10{,}000\) wavelength bins, so there are fewer objects than features. Diagonalizing the covariance matrix costs \(\mathcal{O}(D^3) = \mathcal{O}(10^{12})\) operations, about 17 minutes at \(10^9\) operations per second. The SVD costs \(\mathcal{O}(N^2D) = \mathcal{O}(10^{10})\) operations, about 10 seconds.

The advantage grows as the number of objects falls. With \(N = 100\) spectra and the same \(D\), the SVD costs \(\mathcal{O}(N^2D) = \mathcal{O}(10^8)\) operations, about 0.1 seconds. This is four orders of magnitude fewer than the \(10^{12}\) operations of the diagonalization.

Connection to PCA

With the centered data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\), PCA needs the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S} = (1/N)\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\).

Substituting the SVD of \(\mathbf{X}\) into this expression gives \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S} &= \frac{1}{N}(\mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T)^T(\mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T) \\ &= \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{V\Sigma}^T\mathbf{U}^T\mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T. \end{aligned}\]Since \(\mathbf{U}\) has orthonormal columns, \(\mathbf{U}^T\mathbf{U} = \mathrm{Id}\), and the expression simplifies to \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S} &= \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{V\Sigma}^T\mathbf{\Sigma V}^T. \end{aligned}\]The matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is diagonal with the entries \(\sigma_m^2\), where \(\sigma_m\) are the singular values, because \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is a rectangular diagonal matrix. Therefore \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S} &= \mathbf{V}\left(\frac{1}{N}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right)\mathbf{V}^T \\ &= \mathbf{V}\left(\frac{1}{N}\text{diag}(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2, \ldots, \sigma_D^2)\right)\mathbf{V}^T. \end{aligned}\]

This is the spectral decomposition \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{B}^T\) of Section 10.4 with \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{V}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/N\). The columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) are therefore the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\), which are the principal components, and the eigenvalues are \(\lambda_m = \sigma_m^2/N\). Larger singular values belong to directions of larger variance. The singular values are in descending order, so the eigenvalues are in descending order too. This matches the order of the principal components by explained variance.

Practical Implementation

This relation lets us compute PCA from the SVD without forming the covariance matrix, in four steps.

  1. Center the data matrix \(\mathbf{X}\).

  2. Compute its SVD \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T\).

  3. Use the columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) as the principal components.

  4. Project the data onto these components to get the lower-dimensional representation.

To reduce the dimension to \(M < D\), let \(\mathbf{V}_M\) hold the first \(M\) columns of \(\mathbf{V}\). The projection of the data is \[ \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{V}_M. \]

The SVD already contains the coefficients, so we can obtain them without the matrix product \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}_M\). Substituting \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T\) gives \[ \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{V}_M = (\mathbf{U\Sigma V}^T) \mathbf{V}_M. \]Since \(\mathbf{V}\) is orthogonal, \(\mathbf{V}^T\mathbf{V}_M\) is the \(D \times M\) matrix with the identity \(\mathrm{Id}_M\) on top and zeros below. It selects the first \(M\) columns of \(\mathbf{U\Sigma}\), so \[ \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{U}_M \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_M. \] Here \(\mathbf{U}_M\) holds the first \(M\) columns of \(\mathbf{U}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_M\) is the diagonal matrix of the first \(M\) singular values.

Once the SVD is known, the coefficients \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{U}_M \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_M\) need only a scaling of the columns of \(\mathbf{U}_M\), which costs \(\mathcal{O}(NM)\) operations. Computing \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}_M\) directly multiplies an \(N \times D\) matrix by a \(D \times M\) matrix and costs \(\mathcal{O}(NDM)\) operations.

Reconstruction and Explained Variance

PCA also lets us reconstruct an approximation of the data from the reduced representation. In terms of the SVD of the centered data matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), the coefficients are \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{U}_M\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_M\) and the reconstruction of the centered data is \(\widehat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{V}_M^T = (\mathbf{U}_M \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_M)\mathbf{V}_M^T\). Adding the mean vector \(\overline{\mathbf{x}}\) to each row of \(\widehat{\mathbf{X}}\) gives the reconstruction in the original space.

To choose the number of components to retain, we can also use the singular values to calculate the proportion of variance explained by a component. For the \(m\)-th component it is \[ \text{Explained Variance Ratio}_m = \frac{\sigma_m^2}{\sum_{j=1}^D \sigma_j^2}. \]This equals \(\lambda_m / \sum_j \lambda_j\), because \(\lambda_m = \sigma_m^2/N\). Summing the first \(M\) of these ratios gives the explained variance ratio of the first \(M\) components. By examining this ratio as we add components, we can find how many components capture a desired percentage of the total variance.

The SVD is also more accurate, even when \(N > D\). Forming \(\mathbf{S}\) squares the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, so rounding errors affect the small eigenvalues more. The SVD of \(\mathbf{X}\) avoids this squaring. For these reasons the SVD is the usual choice for computing PCA of high-dimensional data.

10.9 Limitations of PCA

PCA has four limits that matter for astronomical data.

Orthogonality Constraint

PCA requires orthogonal basis vectors, but the directions in feature space along which different physical processes change the data need not be orthogonal. In stellar spectra, for example, temperature and metallicity change many of the same absorption lines, so orthogonal axes can mix them. The first few components carry the most variance, but each can mix several physical parameters. Because the components are orthogonal, one physical parameter can also spread over several components. We should therefore be careful when we give a single component a physical meaning.

Unimodal Assumption

PCA describes the data only through its mean and covariance matrix. The mean and the covariance matrix describe a single, roughly elliptical cluster well. For several clusters PCA gives one common set of directions. Data with several clusters have a multimodal distribution, which has several peaks, or modes (Chapter 9). Two clusters make it bimodal.

Galaxies fall into types such as spiral, elliptical and irregular, and stars form separate groups in parameter space. For such data PCA finds one set of components for all the points together. These components follow the largest total variance, which can differ from the main axis of each cluster. In Figure 10.9 the first component follows the line between the two clusters, and the main axis of each cluster points in another direction.

The problem is largest when the variance within the clusters is smaller than the variance between them, as in the figure. As panel (b) shows, the first principal component mainly carries the variation between the clusters. If we keep only this component, we discard the spread along \(z_2\) within each cluster. Such a loss can hide relations inside a single population.

Sensitivity to Outliers

Because PCA maximizes variance, it is sensitive to outliers. A few extreme points can change the directions of maximum variance, so that the components describe the outliers instead of the typical pattern.

Astronomical data often contain outliers, and many of them are of scientific interest. They can be rare object types, measurement errors or unusual phenomena, and any of them can affect PCA. We can inspect the outliers first. We can remove those that are errors, or use a variant of PCA that gives outliers less weight.

Scale Dependence

PCA depends on the relative scales of the features. A feature with a large numerical range contributes more to the covariance matrix. It can dominate the components, even if it is not the most important feature physically. Changing the unit of one feature changes its variance, and therefore changes the components.

Astronomical measurements often have very different scales, for example magnitudes from 10 to 30 and parallaxes from 0.001 to 0.1. Without rescaling, features with a large range can hide relations in features with a small range. Dividing each centered feature by its standard deviation is a common rescaling, called standardizing.

Alternatives to PCA

Other methods address some of these limits. Independent component analysis (ICA) looks for components that are statistically independent, in place of components of maximum variance. Independent variables have zero mutual information (Chapter 8). The components of ICA need not be orthogonal. When the underlying processes are independent, the components can be easier to interpret physically. In astronomy the method can separate the sources in mixed signals.

Autoencoders are neural networks that describe each object with a few numbers and map it back, and they generalize PCA to nonlinear maps (Chapter 15). They need not keep the orthogonality constraint and can represent more complex relations in the data. Their representations may be easier to interpret physically. They also need more computing time and can fit the noise in the data.

For data with clear clusters, we can first find the clusters with a clustering method (Chapter 11) and then apply PCA to each cluster. Each cluster then has its own mean and its own components. This respects the cluster structure of the data and still reduces the dimension within each population.

PCA describes the data with linear combinations of the features, but astronomical data often form groups. In Chapter 11 we turn to clustering.

10.10 Tutorial: Principal Components of Galaxies

This tutorial applies principal component analysis (PCA) and the singular value decomposition (SVD) of this chapter to images of galaxies. Galaxy shapes depend on how galaxies formed and evolved. The full tutorial can be found at https://statml.org/ as tutorial 10.

Mergers tend to make smooth ellipticals, while gas that settles into a rotating disk forms disk galaxies. A survey takes images of more galaxies than we can examine, and each image has thousands of pixels (top row of Figure 10.10a). We therefore want a few numbers per galaxy, and the images can show which shapes occur.

Learning from images alone is unsupervised learning. The target was a regression value in Section 4.8 and a class in Section 7.10. Here the images have no target to say which pixels matter, so their variation guides us. We keep the directions in the space of pixels along which the images vary most (Section 10.1), because these keep as much information as possible. If a few processes shape the galaxies, most of the variation may lie along a few of these directions.

PCA finds these directions, the principal components, as the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (Section 10.4). The tutorial’s sample has fewer galaxies than pixels, so the SVD of Section 10.8 finds them without the large covariance matrix of the pixels.

The SVD gives the full set of components, so we must still decide how many to keep. Without a target there is no prediction error to guide this choice, so we ask how well the first \(M\) components reconstruct each galaxy. The variance that they miss is the average squared reconstruction error (Section 10.1). The eigenvalues rank the components by variance, so the first \(M\) components miss the least. The share of the total variance that they keep is the explained variance ratio (Section 10.7).

A few components reproduce the overall elongation and orientation of a galaxy, and more add detail (Figure 10.10a). The explained variance ratio rises steeply at first and slowly after, so later components add less (Figure 10.10b). The number to keep therefore depends on how much detail the application needs.

A physical reading of the components needs caution, because PCA chooses orthogonal directions by variance. A few directions with much variance do not show that a few processes shape the galaxies. Because galaxies have different orientations, elongation changes different pixels in each image, so it can spread over several orthogonal components (Section 10.9). Plotted as an image, a component shows a way in which the galaxies vary, and it need not match a physical property.

Once we choose how many components to keep, a galaxy has a few coefficients, its coordinates along them. These summarize it approximately, which is what we wanted. A regression or classification on them has fewer weights than one on the pixels, which can lower the overfitting of Section 4.8. The same approach applies to spectra and light curves, where a compact description lets us study large populations together.

Further Reading

Pearson (1901) found lines and planes of closest fit to points in space. Hotelling (1933) developed principal components as the linear combinations of the variables that carry the most variance. Eckart and Young (1936) showed that the SVD truncated to its largest singular values gives the best least squares approximation with fewer components. Golub and Kahan (1965) and Golub and Reinsch (1970) developed stable algorithms for the SVD, which remain influential in PCA software. Anderson (1958) treats the theory of PCA within multivariate statistics, and Murtagh and Heck (1987) present PCA for astronomers. Jolliffe (2002) covers the theory, variants and uses of PCA. Comon (1994) treats independent component analysis, an alternative for non-Gaussian data. Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006) explored nonlinear dimension reduction with autoencoders, which go beyond linear PCA. The galaxy images of the tutorial are SDSS images from Galaxy Zoo 2, as in Ma et al. (2026).
